notes.title: Chapter map: Turn-taking
notes.html:
This section answers two questions every turn: has the person finished? (endpoint) and should the agent stop talking? (yield). Read it right after Foundations: these two decisions hold most of the time and most of the "it feels wrong" in a voice agent.

Where this sits

capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe

Reading order

# Note Tier Stage You'll understand
1 Endpointing CORE endpoint the min/max wait, one authority, where our 2–3.5 s goes
2 Semantic turn detection CORE endpoint how a model picks the short or long wait, and its two errors
3 Preemptive generation SUPPORTING endpoint hiding the model inside the wait, and why turns must be idempotent
4 Barge-in CORE yield stop on sound, decide on words, record only what was heard
5 Backchannels and overlap SUPPORTING yield vad vs adaptive interruption, why agents don't say "mm-hm"
– Silence and timeouts BREADTH endpoint the check-in ladder when nobody speaks

Owners

Concept Home
min_delay, max_delay, endpointing modes, one authority endpointing
The turn-detector model, audio vs text, its errors semantic turn detection
Layering VAD, detector and window; language-aware pause handling semantic turn detection
Stop, resume, false interruption, truncating the record barge-in
adaptive vs vad interruption, backchannel handling backchannels and overlap
Drafting before commit, turn-keyed state preemptive generation
Pause vs end, backchannel vs interruption (the classes) how people take turns
VAD itself (Silero, frames, thresholds) voice activity detection
Echo cancellation and the server-side echo guard echo cancellation, echo guard
Speculative pre-generation (the design's version) speculative pre-generation

Decide: which turn-detection mode?

Ask in order If yes → mode Because
1. Is the UI push-to-talk? manual (commit_user_turn()) the user marks the end; no guessing
2. Is the model a realtime speech-to-speech model? the model's own detector it hears the audio already
3. Is the language covered by the turn detector? turn detector (default) meaning and prosody, not just silence
4. Otherwise vad, or stt if the STT vendor endpoints well silence or the vendor's signal

🔊 Our system in one table

Stage What we run Status Measured
endpoint inference.TurnDetector(); min_delay 0.8 s, max_delay 3.5 s; Deepgram endpointing off wait p50 2 067 ms (43 calls); mean 2.47 s, median 3.5 s (71 turns, 11–13 Oct)
endpoint preemptive generation on; turn-keyed, idempotent graph hit rate not measured
yield vad mode, 0.4 s, resume after 2.0 s; only played text counts false-interruption rate not measured
yield agent backchannels off –
endpoint silence ladder 10 s / +25 s / +25 s –

Landscape (as of Oct 2026)

Option Who Note
Audio turn detector v1 / v1-mini LiveKit 14 languages; v1 on Cloud inference, v1-mini local CPU
Text turn detector (MultilingualModel) LiveKit deprecated, removal in SDK 2.0; English TNR 87.0%
STT-side endpointing e.g. AssemblyAI, Deepgram Flux (named by LiveKit) turn_detection="stt"; VAD still handles interruptions
Adaptive interruption LiveKit Cloud acoustic model; needs aligned transcripts
Model-side turn-taking realtime and full-duplex models the model decides; less control

Game Day

Q6 user finished · Q7 barge-in · Q32 LLM in the hot path · Q33 turn detector · Q34 interrupt mid-question · Q35 echo as testimony

notes.title: Endpointing — Deciding the Turn Is Over
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Turn-taking tuning (read 16 Oct 2026) · LiveKit — Turn detection & interruptions · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §1 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/03-vad-turn-detection.md

TL;DR

Endpointing turns "the voice stopped" into "the turn is over" by waiting a chosen amount of silence. It is the largest controllable delay in a voice turn, and every setting trades speed against cutting people off.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: VAD: silencedetector: finished?wait min_delaywait max_delayfinal transcript in?commit the turn

Recall

Prompt Answer
What starts the endpoint clock? VAD reporting that speech stopped
What are min_delay and max_delay? the wait when the turn sounds finished, and the longest wait when it doesn't
LiveKit defaults (Oct 2026) 0.5 s / 3.0 s; 0.3 s / 2.5 s with the audio turn detector
Why turn the STT vendor's endpointing off? two authorities disagree; one must decide
What else must arrive before commit? the final transcript
Draw the wait for "finished", "mid-thought" and "transcript late" three bars: min_delay, max_delay, and a commit pushed past the window

The idea

Without it: a fixed silence timer forces one number on everyone. At 150 ms the agent cuts off every thinker; at 500 ms and up it feels slow (interview_prep/03).

It does: waits a short window when the speech sounds finished and a long one when it doesn't, with a semantic model making that call (semantic turn detection).

It costs: the floor is paid on every turn, and the ceiling on every turn the model judges unfinished, right or wrong.

How it works

Rule Because
One authority for end of turn STT endpointing and the agent's detector fire at different times; a turn would commit twice or early
The window is a switch, not a slider in LiveKit a probability under the detector's threshold selects max_delay, anything else min_delay (FLOW §1, reading LiveKit's audio_recognition.py)
The commit also waits for the final words a turn with missing words would be answered wrong

Modes (LiveKit turn_detection, as of Oct 2026): turn detector model (default, recommended) · realtime model's own · "vad" (silence only) · "stt" (the STT vendor's endpointing) · "manual" (push-to-talk, commit_user_turn()).

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
endpointing.min_delay 0.5 s (0.3 s with the audio detector) fewer cut-offs at thinking pauses; paid every turn snappier, more people cut off
endpointing.max_delay 3.0 s (2.5 s with the audio detector) slow thinkers finish trailing answers are cut
endpointing.mode fixed dynamic (Python): adapts within the range from the session's pause statistics –
STT vendor endpointing on in most STT plugins – off: one authority

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
min_delay 0.8 s (ENDPOINT_MIN_S) 0.5 s cut answers at "I used Kubernetes for the…" (FLOW §1)
max_delay 3.5 s (ENDPOINT_MAX_S) the longest wait on an answer that trails off
Deepgram endpointing_ms 0 (off) meghdootam/main.py: the turn detector is the one authority
Endpoint wait p50 2 067 ms, p95 3 640 ms (43 calls, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026) as_built §3
Where it goes floor 37% of turns at 0.8 s · ceiling 39% at 3.5 s (56% of all waiting) · transcript late 23% (31%) FLOW §1: 71 turns, 10 calls, 11–13 Oct 2026, one speaker
max_delay 2.0 s trial mean wait 2.68 → 2.24 s; one paused sentence split into three turns FLOW §1, synthetic caller, 13 Oct 2026; not adopted

Deviation: the design budgets 150–250 ms for this stage; the 0.8 s floor alone is over three times that, chosen to protect answers.

Measure it

  • Metric — end-of-turn wait p50 and p95 (end_of_turn_delay per turn), and the cut-off rate on a labelled set.
  • See it — our log line USER '…' | stt_delay=… eou_delay=…; split turns into floor, ceiling and transcript-late.
  • Bounded by — Chair treats a paused answer as one answer, so an early cut costs a restarted reply, not a skipped question.

Pitfalls

Lowering min_delay to fix latency

  • Why it's tempting: it's the number in front of every turn.
  • Why it's wrong: in our log the ceiling and late transcripts hold 87% of the waiting; 0.8 → 0.5 s saves 0.3 s on a third of turns and brings back cut-offs.
  • Think instead: look at which outcome holds the time; here that is max_delay and the late final transcript.

Leaving STT endpointing on as a backup

  • Why it's tempting: two signals sound safer than one.
  • Why it's wrong: the turn ends on whichever fires first, so the semantic detector's "wait, they're mid-thought" is overruled.
  • Think instead: one authority; let the STT finalise when VAD says speech ended.

Tuning on your own voice

  • Why it's tempting: it's the fastest test loop.
  • Why it's wrong: pause length varies by speaker, language and stress; our log is one speaker and includes probe turns.
  • Think instead: build a labelled set of real answers ("finished or not, by ear") and tune on that.

Connections

… → transcribe → endpoint → think → … — the stage that holds most of the turn's time.

  • asks the semantic turn detector — finished or pausing? It also owns the layered, language-aware pause rules.
  • hides work behind it via preemptive generation.
  • is the biggest line in the latency budget.
  • imitates how people take turns.
  • Say it: Q6 · Q33

notes.title: Semantic Turn Detection — Finished, or Pausing to Think?
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Turn detector (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §1 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §6 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/main.py (turn_handling)

TL;DR

A small model looks at the end of what the person said and predicts whether they have finished. "I think the answer is…" is not finished after 400 ms of silence; "…so I'd shard by tenant." is. The prediction picks the short or the long endpoint wait, so its errors become either cut-offs or dead air.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: silence ≥ 0.25 smodel hears the last audioP(finished)short waitlong wait

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does it predict? whether the speaker has finished their turn
LiveKit's current model reads audio: words plus intonation, pitch and rhythm (no transcript needed)
Variants (Oct 2026) v1 on LiveKit Inference, v1-mini on local CPU
Languages 14, including English and Hindi
What happened to the text model? deprecated, to be removed in SDK 2.0
Draw the two errors on a timeline false "finished": agent talks over a thinker; false "not finished": long silence after a complete answer

The idea

Without it: silence is the only signal, and thinking pauses are as silent as endings.

It does: adds meaning and prosody. A falling pitch on a complete sentence says "done"; a trailing "and the…" says "wait".

It costs: a model call per pause, a dependency on its languages and accents, and errors in both directions that you can only see on a labelled set.

How it works

Audio detector (current) Text detector (deprecated)
Input user audio STT transcript
Hears tone yes no
Runs v1: LiveKit Inference · v1-mini: local CPU local CPU, < 500 MB RAM, 396 MB on disk
Latency not stated; a prediction taking ~1 s commits anyway ~50–160 ms per turn on CPU
Languages 14 incl. Hindi English + 13
Published accuracy none; points to the eot-bench harness English TPR 99.3%, TNR 87.0%
Status default removal in SDK 2.0

All facts from LiveKit's turn-detector page, read 16 Oct 2026. Requires VAD with min_silence_duration ≥ 0.25 s (Silero's default 0.55 s passes). If v1 fails or times out, the session logs once, treats in-flight predictions as finished, and uses v1-mini for the rest of the call.

Best practice: layer the signals, and make the pause rules language-aware.

Layer One job Language-aware how
1. VAD speech or silence, per frame; tuned for the room's noise, not for turn length – (language-independent)
2. Semantic detector finished or holding the floor, from words and prosody per-language unlikely_threshold (LiveKit accepts a dict keyed by language); fillers ("um", "matlab", "toh") hold the floor, and an audio model hears them even when the STT drops them
3. Endpoint window how long to wait for each verdict min_delay / max_delay per language or accent cohort, set from labelled recordings; dynamic endpointing (Python) adapts to this speaker's own pauses
4. Final-transcript gate don't commit with words missing –
Fallback a language the detector doesn't cover vad or stt mode with a longer fixed hangover, not the English-tuned window

Why per language: the typical gap between turns differs across languages (Stivers et al. 2009 found mean gaps from about 7 ms in Japanese to about 470 ms in Danish), and code-switched speech (Hinglish) pauses where neither language alone would. One window tuned on one language cuts off speakers of another.

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
unlikely_threshold (float, or a dict per language) calibrated per model (not listed) more turns judged unfinished: fewer cut-offs, more long waits agent replies more eagerly
version v1 on Cloud; v1-mini outside Cloud – pin v1-mini for local-only, no network call
VAD min_silence_duration Silero 0.55 s detector asked later detector asked sooner (floor 0.25 s)

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Detector inference.TurnDetector() (audio model, Cloud, local fallback) on livekit-agents 1.8.2 meghdootam/main.py
Errors seen complete sentences held the full 3.5 s ("Are you there?", "Three questions."); fragments committed at 0.8 s ("with the") FLOW §1, reading of 71 turns, 11–13 Oct 2026; not a labelled eval
Accent coverage not measured on Indian English decision_rationale weak point 1
Language-aware pauses not built: one language (en-IN), default threshold, one fixed window for everyone meghdootam/main.py
Target window tuned per accent profile on recorded answers; a fixed hangover as the fallback if the model underperforms as_built §2 row 6, design §6.1
Labelled end-of-turn set planned: finished or not, by ear FLOW §1 next step 3

Stale fact to stop repeating: the Game Day voice fact sheet (§7.4) describes a 135M-parameter, English-only text model. That was LiveKit's earlier detector; the build now runs the audio model.

Measure it

  • Metric — on a labelled set: false-finished rate (cut-offs) and false-unfinished rate (turns held to max_delay), per accent cohort.
  • See it — per turn, whether the wait was min_delay or max_delay and what the person said; listen to the ceiling turns.
  • Bounded by — max_delay caps dead air; Chair treats a paused answer as one answer.

Pitfalls

Reading the model's speed as the stage's cost

  • Why it's tempting: inference is tens of milliseconds, so the stage looks cheap.
  • Why it's wrong: the model's output selects a wait of 0.8 s or 3.5 s; the cost is the wait, decided by the model.
  • Think instead: measure how often each wait is chosen, and whether it was right.

Assuming it is English-only

  • Why it's tempting: the earlier LiveKit model was, and older docs still say so.
  • Why it's wrong: the audio detector lists 14 languages including Hindi (Oct 2026); the claim is out of date.
  • Think instead: check the vendor page when you write; what's still unproven is accuracy on our speakers, not language support.

One pause window for every language and accent

  • Why it's tempting: the defaults work in the vendor's demo, and one number is easy to reason about.
  • Why it's wrong: pause norms differ by language and speaker; a window tuned on one cohort cuts off another, which in an interview is a fairness bug, not a UX one.
  • Think instead: per-language thresholds and windows from labelled recordings, cut-off rate reported per cohort, and a longer fixed hangover where the detector doesn't cover the language.

Trusting it without a labelled set

  • Why it's tempting: the vendor calls it the recommended default.
  • Why it's wrong: our log shows errors both ways, and the audio model publishes no accuracy figure.
  • Think instead: label real turns by ear, then compare thresholds and detectors on that set.

Connections

… → transcribe → endpoint → think → … — the decision inside the endpoint wait.

  • chooses the window in endpointing.
  • mirrors, on the other side, backchannel detection — both separate a short sound from a real turn change.
  • replaced by the model's own detector in realtime pipelines.
  • Say it: Q33 · Q6

notes.title: Barge-in — Stopping When the Person Talks Over the Agent
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Turn-taking tuning (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §2 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/04-barge-in.md · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §2 row 11

TL;DR

When the person speaks over the agent, the agent stops its audio at once, then waits to see whether words follow: if they do, the person has the turn; if not, it was noise and the agent resumes. Afterwards, only what the agent actually got out counts as said.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: agent speakingstop audio ─words within timeout?person's turnresume where it stopped

Recall

Prompt Answer
What triggers the stop? VAD (or the adaptive model) hearing the person while the agent speaks
What is a false interruption? a stop with no words after it: noise, a cough
What happens then? the agent resumes after false_interruption_timeout
What goes in the chat history? only the part of the reply that was actually played
How do you protect a line that must be heard whole? speak it with interruptions disabled
Draw a real and a false interruption on one timeline stop at onset; words arrive vs 2 s of nothing then resume

The idea

Without it: the agent talks over the person until its sentence ends, and the transcript says it asked a question the person never heard.

It does: yields the floor within a fraction of a second, decides afterwards whether the yield was real, and truncates the record to what was heard.

It costs: stopping on onset means stopping on noise and on the agent's own echo; every false stop is a broken sentence the person hears.

How it works

Rule Because
Stop on sound, decide on words waiting for a transcript would leave the agent talking for another ~300 ms or more
Truncate the reply to what was played a question cut off before its end was never asked
Some lines are not interruptible a pause or time-limit notice must be heard whole
Echo is a separate defence barge-in fires ~150 ms in, before any transcript exists, so it can't tell echo from voice (voice/echo.py)

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
interruption.mode adaptive if available, else vad – vad: any voice stops it, easy to see working
interruption.min_duration 0.5 s ignores short sounds stops sooner
interruption.min_words 0 (needs STT) waits for words before stopping: fewer false stops, slower –
false_interruption_timeout 2.0 s waits longer for words resumes sooner after noise
resume_false_interruption True – False: a false stop stays stopped
allow_interruptions per say() True – False for lines that must be heard

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Mode vad, min_duration 0.4 s, false_interruption_timeout 2.0 s meghdootam/main.py; chosen so barge-in is visible in a prototype
What counts as asked ctx.spoken: a question cut off before it was heard does not count FLOW §2 step 6, §3
Fixed lines pause and limit lines spoken with allow_interruptions=False FLOW §2
Echo that cut her off dropped by the echo guard; the reply is said again, at most twice FLOW §2 step 5, echo.MAX_RESPEAKS
Target use the voice vendor's own report of what was heard (Flux Interrupt) as_built §2 row 11

A failure this had (real call, 13 Oct 2026): a transcript that arrived after commit interrupted Rachel, the echo guard dropped it, and she went silent. The guard matched letters and judged by commit time; both fixed and checked by playing her own question back at her on a live call (FLOW §2).

Measure it

  • Metric — false-interruption rate (stops with no words), time from onset to silence, and the share of questions marked not-delivered.
  • See it — log false interruption (noise, no words) → resumed=True; for echo, ECHO suppressed (overlap …).
  • Bounded by — resume after the timeout; at most two re-says per reply; uninterruptible fixed lines.

Pitfalls

Waiting for words before stopping

  • Why it's tempting: it removes false stops at one stroke.
  • Why it's wrong: the transcript lags speech by hundreds of milliseconds, so the agent keeps talking over a person who is already speaking.
  • Think instead: stop on sound, then use words to decide whether to resume.

Logging the whole reply as said

  • Why it's tempting: the text was generated, so it's easy to store.
  • Why it's wrong: the person heard half; scoring or planning on the full text assumes a question they never heard.
  • Think instead: store what was played, and let progress count only delivered moves.

Expecting barge-in to handle echo

  • Why it's tempting: the agent's voice in the mic is "just more sound".
  • Why it's wrong: barge-in can't tell it from the person; it stops the agent, and the echo's transcript becomes the person's answer.
  • Think instead: echo cancellation on the device plus a server-side guard on the transcript.

Connections

… → speak → yield → observe — the agent's half of overlap.

  • is tuned against backchannels — "mm-hm" should not stop it.
  • hands the turn to endpointing when words follow.
  • is made harder by preemptive generation — a turn can run twice.
  • Say it: Q7 · Q34 · Q35

notes.title: Backchannels and Overlap — "Mm-hm" Is Not an Interruption
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Adaptive interruption handling (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/07-backchannel-overlap.md

TL;DR

A backchannel ("mm-hm", "right", "okay") tells the speaker to keep going; an interruption takes the floor. Plain VAD can't tell them apart, so an adaptive model listens to the overlapping sound and only stops the agent for a real bid for the turn.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: sound over the agentadaptive model: backchannel?keep speakingbarge-in

Recall

Prompt Answer
Backchannel vs interruption "keep going" vs "my turn"
How LiveKit's adaptive mode decides an acoustic model on the overlapping audio, not the transcript
Where it runs (Oct 2026) LiveKit Cloud inference, on by default there; local dev with a free quota
Why most agents don't backchannel themselves in a cascade the "mm-hm" lands late and interrupts the person
Draw the agent speaking while the person says "mm-hm", in vad and in adaptive mode vad: agent stops mid-word; adaptive: agent keeps going

The idea

Without it: every "yeah" stops the agent mid-sentence; listeners who are engaged get punished for it.

It does: classifies short overlapping sounds before they stop the agent or reach the model.

It costs: a model call on overlap, a Cloud dependency, and a new error: a real interruption judged a backchannel leaves the agent talking over the person.

How it works

Sound over the agent vad mode adaptive mode
"mm-hm", "okay", "right" stops the agent keeps speaking
cough, door stops, resumes after the timeout keeps speaking (or stops and resumes)
"wait, can I ask…" stops stops
the agent's own echo stops (echo guard then drops the transcript) depends; still needs AEC and the echo guard

Adaptive mode (LiveKit, read 16 Oct 2026): needs a VAD, and in a cascade an STT with aligned transcripts (all LiveKit Inference STT models have them; check stt.capabilities.aligned_transcript for plugins). Not compatible with Gemini Live. No latency or accuracy figure is published.

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
interruption.mode adaptive on Cloud when conditions hold, else vad – vad: every voice stops the agent
backchannel_boundary (Python) (1.0 s, 1.0 s) start and end cooldown longer windows treated as backchannel-prone None disables
Agent backchannels none built in – –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Mode vad: a backchannel stops Rachel chosen so barge-in is visible in the prototype (FLOW §2 trade-off)
Agent backchannels off; responsiveness comes from latency, not filler sounds interview_prep/07 §4
Overlap jobs, kept separate who gets the floor (barge-in) · don't score the agent's voice (AEC + echo guard) · who said what (diarization) interview_prep/07 §3

Measure it

  • Metric — barge_in_false_positive_rate (stops caused by backchannels, coughs, echo) and missed real interruptions.
  • See it — LiveKit InterruptionMetrics per event; count false interruption … resumed=True lines.
  • Bounded by — resume after a false stop; vad mode as the fallback when the adaptive model isn't available.

Pitfalls

Making the agent say "mm-hm" to sound human

  • Why it's tempting: people do it, and it signals listening.
  • Why it's wrong: a cascaded agent knows you paused only after transcribing, so its "mm-hm" arrives late and cuts you off.
  • Think instead: buy responsiveness with lower latency; leave agent backchannels to full-duplex models.

Keeping vad mode in production because it worked in testing

  • Why it's tempting: it is simple and visibly reliable.
  • Why it's wrong: real listeners backchannel constantly, and every one breaks the agent's sentence.
  • Think instead: switch to adaptive once barge-in is proven, and measure false stops before and after.

Connections

… → speak → yield — the filter in front of barge-in.

  • filters what reaches barge-in.
  • is the mirror of semantic turn detection — short sound vs real turn change.
  • defined in how people take turns.

notes.title: Preemptive Generation — Starting the Reply Before the Turn Is Confirmed
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Turn-taking tuning (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §3 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/brain/state.py

TL;DR

When a final transcript phrase arrives, start the model on it while the endpoint wait is still running. If the turn commits with the same words, the model's time was hidden inside the wait; if the person keeps talking, throw the draft away and run the turn again.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: final phrasestart draftingturn commits, same words?use the draftdiscard, run again on the fuller text

Recall

Prompt Answer
What starts it? a final transcript before the turn is committed
LiveKit default (Oct 2026) on; preemptive_tts off
What does it cost? wasted model calls when the person keeps talking
What must your code survive? the same turn running twice
How is it different from speculative pre-generation? it drafts on the actual words after a phrase ends; speculation drafts candidates during speech so no call sits on the hot path
Draw a turn that runs twice phrase → draft 1 → more speech → discard → draft 2 → commit → speak

The idea

Without it: the model starts only after the endpoint wait, so its first-token time adds straight onto the turn.

It does: overlaps the model with the wait; on our numbers the wait (seconds) is longer than the first token (~0.45 s), so a hit hides it entirely.

It costs: extra calls, and a rule for every write: a turn may execute more than once.

How it works

Rule (our graph) Because
Every write is keyed by turn and overwrites a re-run replaces its earlier result instead of adding a second one
The move picker reads only earlier turns a re-run must not see its own first decision
Progress is a fold over delivered moves, never a counter a discarded draft, or a question cut off by barge-in, must not advance the plan

Those three rules are an instance of idempotent, event-sourced state: replaying a turn gives the same result.

When it hurts: three cases

Case Example What goes wrong Soften it Ours
Mid-sentence direction change "I'd use Redis… [pause] actually no, Postgres, because…" the draft answers the first half; it's discarded (wasted call) or, if the endpoint commits on the pause, spoken and wrong a longer floor on hesitation words ("actually", "wait", "no"); the semantic detector's mid-thought verdict; never preemptive TTS 0.8 s floor, detector on; discarded drafts re-run on the fuller text
Complex multi-part instructions "Book Tuesday, not Monday, after 3, and email the team" the draft starts on part one and misses later constraints; every new phrase forces a re-draft, up to max_retries skip preemptive for long or list-like turns (max_speech_duration 10 s); confirm back the parts before acting not our case: interview answers, not instructions; the 10 s cap applies
High-accuracy domains medical, legal, payments, scoring a draft built on an interim or a mid-pause transcript may act on words the final transcript changes draft only, never act or speak before commit; re-run on the committed text; keep tools and side effects out of preemptive runs scoring runs on the committed answer; Chair counts only delivered moves; a draft is held until the turn commits and has no side effects outside turn-keyed state

Rule of thumb: preemptive generation is safe when a wrong draft costs only a model call; it's unsafe when a wrong draft can be spoken or can do something.

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
preemptive_generation.enabled True – False: no wasted calls, model time back on the turn
preemptive_tts False True: also starts TTS early, more saved, more waste –
max_speech_duration 10 s longer turns still drafted early long turns skip it
max_retries 3 per turn more re-drafts on long, choppy turns fewer

LiveKit notes it "doesn't always reduce latency" and suggests checking the metrics.

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Preemptive generation on meghdootam/main.py
Safety rules turn-keyed writes, Chair reads prior turns only, delivered() fold FLOW §3; brain/state.py
Speculative pre-generation (the design's version) not built utkarsh_architecture.md §2.1

Measure it

  • Metric — hit rate (drafts used ÷ drafts started), wasted calls per interview, and llm_node_ttft with it on vs off.
  • See it — the same turn number on two CHAIR … lines, the second with more words, then one AGENT … e2e= line.
  • Bounded by — max_retries per turn; turn-keyed writes so a re-run can't double-count.

Pitfalls

Turning it on without making the graph idempotent

  • Why it's tempting: it's one flag.
  • Why it's wrong: a counter like question_index += 1 advances twice on a turn that runs twice; the agent skips a question.
  • Think instead: key every write by turn and count only delivered moves.

Calling it speculative pre-generation

  • Why it's tempting: both start the reply early.
  • Why it's wrong: preemptive still waits for a final phrase and still makes the call after it; speculation prepares replies during speech so the call leaves the hot path.
  • Think instead: preemptive is the cheap first step; measure its hit rate before building speculation.

Connections

… → endpoint → think → … — moves "think" inside the endpoint wait.

  • hides behind the endpoint wait.
  • forces turn-keyed state, which also protects barge-in — cut-off questions don't count.
  • shrinks a line in the latency budget.
  • starts alongside the guard label and background analysis: see Thinking: everything that starts early.
  • is the cheap step before speculative pre-generation.
  • Say it: Q32 · Q3
